title: Satyakama at the teacher's door
hookLine: a boy at a teacher's door is asked his family line, and he doesn't know it
carry: satya: truth made him fit to learn
tomorrow: how can Krishna say he taught the sun?

lines: A BOY AT THE TEACHER'S DOOR.
cards: Every application asks for it somewhere: name, date of birth, parents' names. Now a boy is standing at a teacher's door with one question to answer, and he doesn't know the answer. His name is Satyakama.
He's come to ask the teacher, Gautama, to take him as a student. And the teacher asks what anyone would ask: what's your gotra, your family line? A lie would be easy.

teach.h: I DON'T KNOW YOUR LINE, SON.
teach.b: Back home, he'd already asked his mother, Jabala. In the Chandogya Upanishad she answers plainly: I don't know your line, son. I was young, working as a servant in many houses, when I had you.
I am Jabala; you are Satyakama. Call yourself Satyakama Jabala.

teach.h: HE SAYS IT WORD FOR WORD.
teach.b: So at the door, he says exactly that, word for word. He doesn't polish it. And Gautama says: no one who wasn't a true brahmin could speak like this.
Bring the fuel; I'll take you as a student.

teach.h: YOU HAVE NOT LEFT THE TRUTH.
teach.b: You have not left the truth. Then the teacher sends him off with a herd of thin, weak cows, and Satyakama says he won't come back until the herd has grown.

Out with the cows, the teaching comes to him from strange teachers: a bull, the fire, a swan, a diving bird. When he finally walks home, his teacher looks at him and says: you shine like one who knows Brahman.
So where did this lineage start? Not with a list of names. It started with a sentence that cost something to say.
In this story, the truth was the line. Even his name says it: Satyakama, one who loves the truth.

teach.h: SATYA, NOT BIRTH, OPENS THE DOOR.
teach.b: Many teachers read the story this way: in Hindu teaching, satya, truthfulness, is what makes a student fit to learn about Brahman, more than the family he was born into.

how: Satyakama's story is retold in Hindu homes and classes as a story about truthfulness; some families still ask a person's gotra at weddings and rites, and the story is often brought up beside that custom.

o: a secret name given to a student by a teacher
proof of a noble family needed to study
a teaching that reaches you through a line of people

p: I don't know your line, son
you have not left the truth
the bull, fire, swan, diving bird
teach him out with the cows

s: Satyakama gives a noble family line to get accepted
he repeats his mother's words exactly: she doesn't know his line.
the teacher accepts him because he told the truth
you have not left the truth: bring the fuel.
in the story, only human teachers teach Satyakama
a bull, the fire, a swan and a diving bird teach him first.

games.q: you're Satyakama at the teacher's door. he asks your family line, and you don't know it. what do you say?
o: exactly what your mother told you.
a respectable line nobody will check.
games.why: he tells it word for word. Gautama: no one who wasn't a true brahmin could speak like this. you have not left the truth.

practice: Look at one thing near you that came to you from someone: a photo, a ring, a cup, a book. Don't weigh what it's worth. Let what you know of its story, and what you don't, sit there with you while you breathe.

wordCard.voice: A lineage: in Satyakama's story, a line of teaching that begins with a boy telling the truth about not knowing his own.

orig.note: Sanskrit: a family line; what Gautama asks Satyakama at the door.

carryVoice: Your line: satya, truth made him fit to learn. Sometimes a lineage starts with one honest sentence at a door. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 4.4.1–4.4.5 (Satyakama asks his mother Jabala his gotra; she does not know: in youth, going about much as a servant, she had him; she is Jabala, he is Satyakama; he says the same to Haridrumata Gautama, who says none but a brahmin could speak so, bring the fuel, I will initiate you, you have not gone from the truth; he is given lean, weak cows and will not return until they have multiplied)
Chandogya Upanishad 4.5–4.9 (the bull, the fire, a swan and a diving bird teach him; his teacher: you shine like one who knows Brahman)
